title: H-1B Workers Face Tighter Access on Two Fronts: Job-Loss Grace Period and Visa Interviews
excerpt: A new proposal would erase the 60-day grace period that lets laid-off H-1B, L-1, O-1 and TN workers find a new sponsor, while a separate State Department change forces them into in-person consulate interviews.
body:
• The Trump administration has proposed eliminating the 60-day grace period, in place since 2017, for H-1B, L-1, O-1 and TN workers after a job loss; under the proposal, workers would fall out of status when employment ends.
  • Effective September 2, the State Department curtailed visa interview waivers expanded under the Biden administration: H-1B, L-1 and F-1 applicants must now attend in-person consulate interviews, with waivers limited mostly to diplomats and tourist-business renewals within 12 months of expiration.
  • The twin moves compress both ends of the hiring pipeline for staffing firms and tech employers — less margin to keep workers legal between jobs, longer waits to get them stamped abroad — on top of a litigated $100,000 charge for H-1B admissions.
  • The measures run on different clocks: the grace-period elimination is a proposal still facing rulemaking, while the interview-waiver rollback is already in force — and House lawmakers warn it could derail fall enrollment of Indian students at U.S. universities.

The two moves

The Trump administration is tightening foreign workers' access to the United States on two fronts at once. The Department of Homeland Security has proposed eliminating the 60-day grace period that lets H-1B, L-1, O-1 and TN visa holders remain in the country after a job loss. Separately, the State Department has already curtailed visa interview waivers that let many of those workers renew visas without a consulate visit — in force since September 2. One move compresses the runway at home; the other lengthens the wait abroad.

Front one: no grace after the last paycheck

The proposed rule, set for publication in the Federal Register on September 11, would apply to H-1B, L-1, O-1 and TN workers and their dependents. Since 2017, a laid-off worker has had up to 60 days to find another sponsoring employer, switch status, or leave. Under the proposal, employment ends and lawful status ends with it: a worker cut on a Friday would fall out of status almost immediately, and those who stay could be issued a Notice to Appear, the document that starts deportation proceedings. DHS wrote that the jobs could go to American workers instead: "DHS presumes that they will either offer the same jobs to equally qualified U.S. workers or go through the I-129 petition process."

Concretely: an engineer on an H-1B laid off in a restructuring round currently has two months to line up a new sponsor; under the proposal, the family's legal footing evaporates with the final paycheck — including H-4 dependents whose right to live and, in some cases, work in the U.S. rides on the principal visa holder.

Front two: back to the consulate window

The State Department, in a July 25 website update, narrowed interview-waiver eligibility broadened under Biden. Effective September 2, H-1B, L-1 and F-1 applicants must attend in-person interviews; waivers are now limited largely to government officials and to tourist and business-visitor renewals within 12 months of expiration. The default shortcut is gone — along with the main tool that had kept visa stamping from piling up at understaffed posts. House lawmakers warned the backlogs could derail fall enrollment of Indian students at U.S. colleges.

The change lands directly on travel: a worker visiting family in India who needs a fresh H-1B stamp must now clear an in-person interview before flying back, risking delays or extended administrative processing. Immigration lawyers are advising employers to build redundancy — checking O-1 eligibility, accelerating PERM and I-140 filings to buy time, and using L-1 intracompany transfers as a parallel track.

Context & background

Both moves fit a broader administrative squeeze since January: paused immigrant-visa appointments at U.S. missions, suspended green cards for applicants from 75 countries, and a litigated $100,000 charge to admit H-1B workers. The H-1B program, capped at 85,000 visas a year and heavily used by tech companies and staffing firms, is the common thread: the interview change hits the workers already here, and the grace-period proposal hits the ones between jobs.

Diaspora angle

Indian nationals are the largest single group of H-1B holders, and the one-two punch lands directly on them: in-person consulate interviews to get back into the U.S., and no 60-day cushion after a layoff.

What's next

The fronts move on different clocks. The interview-waiver rollback is already in force, so the question is how fast backlogs build and whether posts add capacity. The grace-period elimination is only a proposal: it must survive rulemaking, including public comment — and given the litigation trailing the administration's other immigration measures, a court challenge is easy to imagine.
